etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English harvest, hervest, from Old English hærfest (“autumn, harvest-time; August”), from Proto-West Germanic *harbist, from Proto-Germanic *harbistaz (“harvest-time, autumn, fall”), from *harbaz, from Proto-Indo-European *kerp-.

definitions.definition: (agriculture) The process of gathering the ripened crop; harvesting.
The yield of harvesting, i.e., the gathered crops or fruits.

quote.citation: 1907 January, Harold Bindloss, chapter 20, in The Dust of Conflict, 1st Canadian edition, Toronto, Ont.: McLeod & Allen, →OCLC:
quote.text: Hester Earle and Violet Wayne were moving about the aisle with bundles of wheat-ears and streamers of ivy, for the harvest thanksgiving was shortly to be celebrated, while the vicar stood waiting for their directions on the chancel steps with a great handful of crimson gladioli.

The frizzle-headed man-eaters were loath to leave their fleshpots so long as the harvest of human carcases was plentiful. Sometimes, when the harvest was too plentiful, they imposed on the missionaries by letting the word slip out that on such a day there would be a killing and a barbecue.

quote.citation: c. 1598–1600 (date written), William Shakespeare, “As You Like It”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene v]:
quote.text: To glean the broken ears after the man / That the main harvest reaps.

definitions.definition: (by extension) The product or result of any exertion or course of action; reward or consequences.

quote.citation: 1655, Thomas Fuller, The Church-history of Britain; […], London:  […]  Iohn Williams […], →OCLC, (please specify |book=I to XI):
quote.text: The pope's principal harvest was in the jubilee.
the harvest of a quiet eye

definitions.definition: The season of gathering ripened crops; specifically, the time of reaping and gathering grain.
(UK, dialectal) The third season of the year; autumn; fall.
(paganism) A modern pagan ceremony held on or around the autumn equinox, which is in the harvesting season.
(transitive) To bring in a harvest; reap; glean.
(transitive) To take a living organism as part of a managed process to gather food or resources, often with the intention of maintaining a healthy population.
(intransitive) To be occupied bringing in a harvest.
